title: Banana peels for Krishna
hook: Krishna turns down a palace feast and eats at a humble house, where he's handed the peels
carry: bhava: god takes the feeling, not the finish

segments.voice: Yesterday: the butter thief, honored as God. Close enough to scold. Today, Krishna grown up, turning down the best dinner in the city.

Remember day seventy-five: Krishna in Hastinapura, asking for peace. Duryodhana has laid out a feast to win him over, gold plates, every dish the palace kitchens can make. Krishna says no. In the Mahabharata he puts it plainly: people eat at someone's table out of love, or out of need, and here there's neither. Then he walks across the city to the small house of Vidura, the old king's wise, humble half-brother. Nobody there is expecting God for dinner.
screen: `A FEAST TO WIN KRISHNA OVER.` → `NOT LOVE, NOT NEED: REFUSED.` → `TO VIDURA'S SMALL HOUSE INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: Families love to tell what happened next, in a telling sung in devotional songs more than written in the epic. Vidura's wife is home when Krishna walks in, and she's so overjoyed she can't think straight. She sits him down, grabs some bananas, peels them, and in her excitement throws the fruit aside and hands him the peels. And Krishna eats them, one after another, smiling, as if he's never tasted anything better. When Vidura gets home he's horrified, and serves the fruit properly. Krishna takes a bite and says, gently, it isn't as sweet as the peels. That's the teaching, and it has a name: bhava, the feeling inside an offering. An old Sanskrit saying makes the same point with a grammar joke: one person says Vishnu's name with the ending wrong, a scholar says it right, and both earn the same, because God takes the feeling. It's why Hindus worship the way they do. Today's word, murti, is a form God is invited into. A temple murti may be carved by trained hands, but in many pujas Ganesha is first called into a little cone of turmeric paste, or a single betel nut. No trunk, no ears. Shiva is honored as a smooth stone. Now, a kitchen table, the week before Ganesh Chaturthi. Someone has made a clay Ganesha for the family shrine. The trunk leans; one ear is bigger. Next to the perfect ones online it looks clumsy, and the worry comes: am I doing this wrong? Krishna ate the peels. The feeling is the offering; the clay carries it.
screen: `VIDURA'S WIFE HANDS HIM PEELS.` · `NOT AS SWEET AS THE PEELS.` · `BHAVA: THE FEELING INSIDE THE OFFERING.` · `MURTI: A FORM GOD IS INVITED INTO.` · then, large: `GOD TAKES THE FEELING, NOT THE FINISH.`

segments.voice: This is the oldest offering there is. Pick one small thing you can give: a flower, a piece of fruit, a spoon of something you cooked, or just a glass of water. Notice the voice that says it isn't enough, not fancy, not done right; let it talk. Then picture Vidura's wife, so happy she handed God the peels, and Krishna smiling as he ate. If you have a shrine or a picture of God at home, set your offering before it with both hands, the way families offer food before a meal, and say a name you love, Krishna or Ganesha, once. If you don't pray, set it down for someone you love, a parent or a friend, and give it with your whole heart. Either way, the gift is the feeling. Stay with that for a few breaths.
Murti. A form, a body: the shape God is invited into, from carved stone to a cone of turmeric, honored for the love inside it. Today's word.
Your line: bhava, God takes the feeling, not the finish. Krishna ate the peels. On to day eighty-seven.
